reference.source: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
clinicalPearls: The commonest lacunar syndrome, classically caused by a small deep infarct in the posterior limb of the internal capsule or the basis pontis.
Weakness affects the face, arm and leg roughly equally on one side, without sensory loss, visual field defect, aphasia or neglect.
The complete absence of 'cortical' signs (aphasia, apraxia, agnosia, hemianopia, gaze deviation) is what distinguishes it from a cortical territory infarct.
Dysarthria and mild transient sensory symptoms may occur, but objective sensory loss argues against the pure motor label.
Small-vessel lipohyalinosis and microatheroma from chronic hypertension and diabetes are the dominant mechanisms rather than embolism.
A capsular warning syndrome, with stuttering, fluctuating or crescendo hemiparesis, heralds impending completed capsular infarction and warrants urgent attention.
CT is frequently normal acutely; diffusion-weighted MRI best demonstrates the small deep infarct and excludes mimics.
Long-term management centres on aggressive control of blood pressure, glycaemia and lipids plus antiplatelet therapy.
reference.pathophysiology: Pure motor hemiparesis results from occlusion of a single small penetrating (perforating) artery supplying the corticospinal tract where its fibres are compactly arranged, most often the lenticulostriate branches to the posterior limb of the internal capsule or paramedian pontine perforators from the basilar artery. Chronic hypertension and diabetes drive lipohyalinosis and microatheromatous change within these end-arteries, producing a small (typically under 15 mm) ischaemic cavity or lacune. Because the lesion lies in white matter tracts distant from cortex, motor fibres to face, arm and leg are interrupted together while sensory, visual and higher cortical pathways are spared, giving the characteristic isolated motor deficit.
additionalDifferentials: Cortical (large-vessel) infarct with predominant motor involvement
Small deep intracerebral haemorrhage in the capsule or pons
Subdural haematoma or mass lesion compressing the internal capsule
Todd's paresis following a focal seizure
Demyelinating lesion of the corticospinal tract
additionalInvestigations: Diffusion-weighted and T2/FLAIR MRI of the brain
Non-contrast CT head to exclude haemorrhage acutely
Vascular imaging of carotids and intracranial vessels to seek an alternative embolic source
ECG and prolonged rhythm monitoring for atrial fibrillation
Fasting glucose, HbA1c and lipid profile
Blood pressure profiling including ambulatory measurement
redFlags: Stuttering or crescendo weakness suggesting capsular warning syndrome and impending completed infarct
Depressed conscious level or headache raising suspicion of haemorrhage
Rapid worsening with new cortical signs indicating larger-territory ischaemia
Fever or systemic sepsis suggesting an alternative or infective cause
reference.prognosis: Functional recovery is often good, with many patients regaining substantial motor function, but recurrent lacunar events and vascular cognitive impairment are common without rigorous risk-factor control. The capsular warning syndrome carries a high short-term risk of completed disabling infarction.
pitfalls: Labelling a stroke 'pure motor' when subtle objective sensory loss or a visual field defect is present, which points instead to a larger lesion.
Assuming a normal acute CT excludes stroke and thereby missing a small deep infarct visible only on diffusion MRI.
Attributing all deficits to small-vessel disease and failing to screen for a treatable embolic source.
Overlooking a small capsular or pontine haemorrhage that can mimic the syndrome exactly.
Under-treating vascular risk factors because the initial deficit seems mild.
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
Fisher CM. Lacunar strokes and infarcts (historical descriptions)
management: Deliver acute ischaemic stroke care on a stroke unit, offering intravenous thrombolysis when the patient presents within the treatment window and haemorrhage is excluded
Start antiplatelet therapy for secondary prevention once haemorrhage is excluded
Control vascular risk factors rigorously with blood-pressure lowering, statin therapy and management of diabetes, the dominant small-vessel mechanisms
Recognise the capsular warning syndrome of stuttering hemiparesis as high-risk, managing urgently with intensified antiplatelet therapy and close monitoring
Provide early multidisciplinary rehabilitation with physiotherapy and occupational therapy to regain motor function
Investigate for an alternative embolic source with vascular imaging and rhythm monitoring where the picture is atypical
Promote smoking cessation and other lifestyle modification to reduce recurrence
